For TPG, shares are down almost 40% YTD alongside pressure on the broad alternative asset manager sector over concerns that the 15%+ annual growth it has seen over the last 3 years is unsustainable. But Alex Blostein expects base management fee growth of ~20% yoy in both 2026E and 2027E as AUM grows in its flagship private equity (PE) funds, investments in its Credit funds leads to management fee realization, and Real Estate fundraising begins contributing to management fees and fee related earnings (FRE). For TSN, Leah Jordan is looking for above consensus earnings growth at the US's largest protein processor and marketer — driven by its diversified protein portfolio, plus further margin expansion owing to ongoing operational improvements, strong demand trends, as well as generally better execution across the board. The US Conviction List – Directors’ Cut was first launched on June 1, 2023 with the objective of providing investors with a curated list of the 20-25 highest conviction and most differentiated fundamental Buy ratings from our US stock coverage.

As we do during these anniversary editions, we provide insight into our stock picking process, review performance (including our most frequently requested ‘portfolio’ performance chart) and reflect on what we learned this past year as we continuously tweak our process with the goal of improving outcomes. Additionally, we summarize the 5 themes we are monitoring as we continue to seek alpha across the US equity investment universe and provide write-ups of the thesis for each stock currently on the list.
Since our last annual publication, the S&P 500 is up
. As we discuss within, the hit rate on ideas during that time (trailing twelve months) has hovered around

against all metrics we track and our equal-weighted indexed return was 180bps below the broader S&P 500 (up 760bps vs the equal weighted index). Consistent with the broader market, the moves under the surface haven't been as smooth as the generally in-line performance would suggest. Our best month was February, where the list benefited from broader participation across market constituents and some strong idiosyncratic alpha on the back of December earnings reports (KEYS, HSY, BRX), while our worst was this past month (May) where the list's underexposure to the technology verticals driving the broader market led to underperformance and a low hit rate.

During the course of the last 12 months, we succeeded in identifying names that showed positive earnings surprises (~80% of names on the list the last 12 months beat their first quarter expectation after list inclusion), but in a market where themes have often trumped numbers, stocks that were in sectors that, for now, are more of a source of funds underperformed. We show this in more detail on page 12. We did have many idiosyncratic successes, where the key fundamental drivers our analysts were looking for materialized (e.g. WMT, HLI, HSY, COF, WWD, PM) and where market themes supplemented our analysts differentiated fundamental view (e.g. KEYS, GEV). In these cases upward earnings revisions led to higher share prices. There were undoubtedly many others that didn’t work out and we show all adds and removals along with performance of each in exhibit 10.

Oversight of the list rests with a subcommittee of our Investment Review Committee — a team of senior research managers who source top ideas from each sector analyst but own the decision to add or remove a name from the list. The list is updated at least once a month in a published note.

As highlighted in each summary write-up, the committee seeks to identify investment views with high conviction, unique points of differentiation, a visible catalyst path and high risk-adjusted return potential. Our goal has been to remain disciplined around our stock selection process, while limiting the list to between 20-25 Buy recommendations and inviting the “competition for capital” among our analysts that many investors have to contemplate.

Since inception, this active discipline has served us well — helping us avoid drawdowns in some names after stated catalysts had passed or market views had become more closely aligned with those of our analysts. But lessons were also learned, as in other instances we would have been better served rotating out of names sooner. As with any investment process we continue to hone our approach, learning from what we got wrong while trying to mimic what we got right.

The S&P 500 is now up 84% since Chat GTP was introduced to the world on November 30, 2022. The move has not been straight up. We had to get through the March ‘23 regional banks crisis, the August 2024 Japan taper tantrum, April ‘25’s Liberation Day, and this year’s US-Iran War. But the bounces off of intermittent bottoms have been swift and determined —each time compelling the market back up to new all-time highs.

Underlying this 3½ year rally has, of course, been the AI infrastructure trade compelled by the world's overwhelming hunger for compute power (and everything that goes with it) to run new artificial intelligence models that hold the promise of improving corporate productivity, streamlining almost everything we do, and who knows what else. As with any demand surge, however, investors are left to assess whether the surge has a cyclical component, can actually be fulfilled, and whether the product underlying the demand holds the promise that so many feel it does today (remember iPads, the Metaverse, and ISP's?).

The 20th century Catholic Trappist monk, Thomas Merton, famously said: ‘You cannot be a man of faith unless you know how to doubt.’ And it is this doubt that sometimes extends and fuels stock market rallies like the one we have seen over the past 3+ years.

As for stocks today, Ben Snider points out that, so far, faith has not had to play as big of a role in the rally as you might think (see the May-26 note, “Earnings growth paves a bumpy path to higher returns”). Our recently raised 8000 year-end 2026 S&P 500 target requires no P/E multiple expansion from here — just the realization of the 24% EPS growth rate that we forecast we are on pace to achieve this year. And, indeed, earnings growth has fueled most of the 84% rally we have seen since November 30 2022. In the December 2, 2022 “US Weekly Kickstart,” David Kostin (our strategist at the time) was forecasting 2023 EPS of $224 for the S&P 500. Fast forward to today, and Ben Snider is forecasting 2026 EPS of $340 — 52% higher than the forward forecast before ChatGTP was introduced. So almost 2/3s of the gain in the S&P 500 over these past 3½ years is coming from plain old earnings. The rest: faith.

Is this faith sustainable? Well if you are a follower of Thomas Merton, there appears to be just enough doubt to keep fueling the faith. Doubts are likely to persist about how much of an impact AI can have outside of the AI ecosystem itself. Jim Covello, writes in a presentation-style report from Apr-30, “AI Spend vs Benefit,” that the key question that needs to be answered for investors to understand how and where to invest going forward is ‘where is the value going to accrue in the supply chain?’ Will value accrue to the enterprise layer, the model layer, the hyperscaler layer, or the chip layer?

And in a May-5 cross-sector Technology note, Jim Schneider, Eric Sheridan, and Gabriela Borges highlight how the next leg of the AI infrastructure cycle is poised to see an explosion in required compute power in “Decoding the Agentic Economy – The Coming Inflection in AI Usage and Margins.” Agentic AI should drive an increase in token consumption of 24-times the current level. And the types of semis to provide these tokens (a term used to describe what a computer needs to generate or consume the equivalent of 3-4 words of data) is likely to be more CPUs than the GPUs that have dominated the AI infrastructure build-out so far.

Finally, to provide further perspective on how difficult it is for markets to identify structural shifts versus cyclical impulses, the relentless march up in AMZN shares over the past 20 years provides another interesting illustration. On May 14, 2007, our then-internet analyst, Anthony Noto, was forecasting AMZN to generate $1.44 in EPS for CY2007 (see the May 14, 2007 note, “Noto’s Internet Notables”). Since that note was published, however, AMZN underwent a series of stock splits equating to a 20:1 split, implying that the $1.44 in 2007 is equivalent to $0.07 on today’s AMZN share base. Fast forward to today, and Eric Sheridan is forecasting AMZN to generate 2026e EPS of $9.02 — 129X what it was earning 19 years ago (see Eric Sheridan’s Apr-30 note, “AMZN: Q1’26 Review: Investing Behind Secular Growth Themes Across Compute, Commerce & Advertising”). On May 14, 2007 AMZN shares traded at a current equivalent of $3.09. Today, the stock trades at $272 — 88X higher. The stock still hasn’t kept up with the earnings growth it has realized over the past 19 years. Where there is faith, doubt resides.

Where does that leave us today? Ben Snider recognizes that the strength of the recent Momentum-driven rally and midterm election seasonality suggest some tactical hedging may be prudent at this time. But we also think the market moves higher from here. Lean into stocks with the strongest earnings growth momentum, including those exposed to the AI infrastructure build-out (see Schneider and team's note above). And also lean into equities with earnings tailwinds and minimal correlation to the AI trade.

We also sat down with Pete Callahan, the US Technology, Media and Telecommunications sector specialist within GS Global Banking & Markets, last week to discuss how the Tech trade is shaping up as we exited May and looked forward to June (see “The Markets: Why There May Be More Investment Opportunities in Internet Stocks”). Where’s the trade? Callahan likes Internet stocks. DASH is on our Conviction List.

Investors are looking at the current market as one big trade wrote Ben Snider in a May-15 note, “AI, Momentum, and the One Big Trade.” And if there is any truth to that sentiment, markets perhaps don’t need 10 themes to focus on. So in our half-time update for 2026, we focus on 5 themes for a ‘one big trade’ market.

1. AI & Power. This was the number one theme going into the year, continues to be the number one theme, and is, of course, what investors are referring to when they say the market is ‘one big trade.’ Jim Schneider and team paved a path for where the AI infrastructure theme may go in the years ahead in a May-5 note, “Decoding the Agentic Economy - The Coming Inflection in AI Usage and Margins.” As AI developers shift their attention towards creating agents that carry out tasks on their own, the compute power infrastructure underlying that shift changes as well, in favor of CPU intensity over GPU intensity. The need to electrify massive new data centers, however, does not abate and in February, Carly Davenport raised our US power demand CAGR by 60bp to 3.2% — this is following two decades of no growth at all (see the Feb-23 note, “Power SD Update: Raising US Demand CAGR to 3.2% on Higher Data Center Load, and Introducing Behind the Meter Assumptions”). CL stocks with direct exposure to AI + Power: AVGO, CLS, DUK, and NVT.

2. Productivity & margin gains. Closely associated with the #1 theme is our new #2 theme, as we are seeing increasing interest from investors in uncovering stocks that are boosting margins through all sorts of productivity initiatives, including the deployment of AI. Snider pointed out in a May-26 note, “Earnings growth paves a bumpy path to higher returns,” that the MEDIAN stock in the S&P 500 reported a 14% boost in EPS for 1Q26. There are not 250 stocks participating in AI infrastructure construction. Joseph Briggs writes that companies that more effectively deploy AI agents are likely to pull away from their industry peers and emerge as the next ‘superstar’ firms in a May-12 economics note, “AI Agents, Intangible Capital, and the Next Superstars.” As we continue to cycle through 2026 and into 2027, ‘margin power’ — the ability to improve profitability through more than just topline growth or pricing power — is likely to gain importance. Stocks on the CL that are not part of the AI or Energy trade but where our analysts are still forecasting significant margin expansion in 2026 include: CFG, LOAR, JNJ, UNH, and XYZ.

3. Inflation & rates. In the first 5 months of 2026, the average price of gasoline in the US has risen by over 50%, driving CPI inflation up to 3.8% in April from 2.7% in December. And alongside this inflation surge, yields on 10-year Treasuries have risen over 30bp to 4.48%. Energy stocks on the list that benefit from the underlying inflation surge, include: COP, GLNG, and DUK. Financials stocks that can see higher profits from a steeper rate curve include CFG, IBKR, and XYZ.

4. Consumer Resilience. A companion theme to inflation & rates is the consumer. But what is perhaps most surprising this year is to see how resilient the US consumer has been in the face of such a stiff inflation headwind. Joseph Briggs highlights the resilient consumer in a May-27 note, “US Consumer Dashboard: May 2026: Low

Confidence.” Real PCE growth is tracking at a healthy 2.1% yoy pace through March and April retail sales were strong. But our economists forecast PCE growth to slow sharply from here as the weight of the energy crisis bears down, and the lift from tax cuts fades. Against this backdrop, Kate McShane and team lower our savings rate forecast to make room for lower income growth but still forecast 2026 discretionary cash flow growth to DECELERATE to 4.2% from 5.1% a year ago in an Apr-28 update, “State of the US Consumer: Lowering our DCF outlook based on lower disposable income expectations.” On the CL, we look for idiosyncratic consumer stocks that can still grow earnings in what might become a less attractive consumer environment. CL stocks with exposure to the US consumer: DKS, TSN, BRX, DASH, XYZ, and even CWST (through housing exposure).

5. Geo-political uncertainty & remilitarization. For the remainder of the year, we feel comfortable combining two themes from our January note into one theme today as policy meets military action creating a symbiotic theme for investors. The remilitarization theme that was in full swing in places like Germany and Japan back in January now includes a major remilitarization in the US highlighted by the US-Iran war — an event we did not anticipate. Unanticipated events also underpin the ‘geopolitical uncertainty’ side of this theme for investors. We do not know when the Strait of Hormuz will reopen. That said, although the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed, physical Brent prices remain well below their early-April highs, driven by substantial OECD strategic reserve releases and a lack of appetite from China refineries writes Yulia Grigsby in a May-20 update, “Oil Tracker: Visible Stock Draws Accelerate on Lower Exports; Weakening China Imports and Demand.” Stocks with exposure to ongoing geopolitical uncertainty and the militarization of the world, include: COP, GLNG, and APD.

title_content.content: Listening in - Inside the Model, On the Road & Everywhere Else

paragraph_content.content: The way we consume media, news, and research has changed meaningfully over the past few years. No longer confined to print — physical or digital — we increasingly consume content through podcasts, videocasts, and even social media. Beginning with the launch of Research Unplugged in 2020, we have expanded our audio footprint as well, adding two new podcast formats in the past year alone. In a recent note, “Listening in at GS: Inside the Model, On the Road & Everywhere Else,” we highlight some of our podcasts that dive deep into the factors that actually drive stock performance (Inside the Model), some of the ways we discover those inputs (On the Road with GS), the themes and topics that matter most to markets today (Research Unplugged), plus a whole bunch more.

item_content.content: - You can find all of our podcasts and similar insights on the “Global Market Intelligence” page, or each of the regional Market Intelligence pages.
- You can find all of our audio content, from podcasts to replays, on the “Audibles” page.

paragraph_content.content: Reflection on what we got right and perhaps more importantly, what we got wrong, is important to our process. Last year, we highlighted in our “lessons learned” that in many cases we would’ve been better served by sticking with winners for longer and removing underperformers earlier. We update this analysis below with that same conclusion, though with improved discipline – the average name that outperformed was on the list for 249 days before being removed vs 194 days for those that underperformed. While we manage this list as a bottom-up list of single stock ideas, agnostic to sector verticals, we did do a better job of ‘respecting what the market told us’ (another lesson learned last year) as we sought to ensure broader representation across market cap and industry groups, though as indicated, our underexposure to the narrow sectors driving the market has hurt overall list performance, as has our attempt to find value in some sectors where business models/exposures are being questioned.

This year we add two new learnings - a refocus on the adage that earnings drive stocks and the challenges one sees when trying to generate alpha when alpha can only be generated when a negative is disproved and when that negative could take years to be proven wrong.

1. Sticking with winners helped overall alpha; we should have cut losses sooner. A repeat from last year, this is core to generating aggregate alpha and is one of the harder disciplines to maintain. We have noted in the past that behavioral biases suggest one may opt to book profits when stocks do well and succumb to thesis drift when a catalyst breaks the wrong way. We attempt to mitigate these behaviors and hold ourselves accountable as we see the analysts' thesis play out in the numbers.

In August of 2014, we published a report that discussed common behavioral biases that can exist in one's investment process (“Mind your Alpha: Case Studies of Behavioral Biases”). One of these was the market's tendency to fade their modeling of companies that have exhibited peer-leading growth — expressing a view that the relative strength of the past cannot last. We used sales growth as the catalyst metric on which we based our analysis. The conclusion: there is a high persistence rate for companies that beat consensus expectations on revenues in a given year that suggests they will beat again in subsequent years.

This bias can be measured in shorter time periods and with a different key performance indicator (KPI). In our June 2025 report, we ran a similar analysis on Directors' Cut stocks we had on the list for at least one earnings report since the inception of the list. In this report, we run this for the 49 stocks that were on the US Conviction List during the trailing 12 months (TTM) and also on the list for at least one earnings report. Key takeaways from this include:

item_content.content: Our analysts have been good at picking fundamental earnings winners. 78% of the TTM new adds (38 stocks) beat consensus EPS estimates in the 1st quarter they reported after being added to the list.
Those stocks outperformed. Those 38 stocks on average outperformed the S&P 500 by 215bps in the 6-day period of -3/+3 days around earnings, with 58% of these stocks outperforming the index.

It paid to hold winners. Of the 38 stocks that beat earnings in that first quarter, 28 remained on the list three months later for another quarter of earnings reports (their 2nd; and another 5 current CL ideas have yet to report their 2nd quarter of earnings). 24 of them (86%) beat consensus EPS for a 2nd time. These stocks, that beat again, on average outperformed the S&P 500 by nearly 500 bps during the -3/+3 day window with 75% of them outperforming the index.

And again. Of the 24 that beat for a 2nd time, 14 remained on the CL for a 3rd quarter of earnings (5 current CL ideas have yet to report their 3rd quarter earnings). 12 of these stocks (or 86%) beat consensus again and, on average, generated another 92 bps of alpha vs the S&P 500 in that same 6-day window.

We should have cut losses sooner. 11 stocks missed EPS in their first quarter while on the list losing, on average, 96 bps of relative performance in the -3/+3 days around that event. We only removed 1 of those stocks. 9 of the remaining 10 reported a 2nd quarter, and 5 of them missed again. While only 1 of these stocks underperformed in that same 6-day window, the average relative performance of these stocks (+213bps) was lower than those that beat in two consecutive quarters (+499bps). Of the 5 stocks that missed for a second time, 3 have since reported a 3rd quarter. 2 of these stocks missed and diluted list performance by 800 bps on average. While we try to be disciplined and each case presents different fact patterns, this analysis acts as a good reminder that there is often persistency and consistency in reporting trends.

Applying this analysis to all Directors' Cut stocks we have had on the list since inception and that had reported at least one quarter of earnings (112 stocks), we find that the above conclusions hold true on a life-to-date basis as well. Specifically:

item_content.content: Among the stocks that beat consensus EPS estimates in the 1st quarter and remained on the list for another quarter of earnings, 83% beat again (+325bp average SPX-relative performance); and for those that remained for a 3rd quarter, 88% beat again (+125bp of SPX-relative outperformance).

Among the stocks that missed in the 1st quarter and remained on the list for another quarter of earnings, 61% missed again (-154bp average SPX-relative performance); and for those that remained for a 3rd quarter, 80% missed again -550bp of SPX-relative outperformance).

paragraph_content.content: Stocks on the CL as of May 31 that beat consensus estimates in two or more consecutive quarters: APD, BRX, CLS, DUK, GLNG, JNJ, KTB, and NVT. Stocks that missed in consecutive quarters: ARES and WYNN (two quarters), both of which we removed in this monthly update.

We find a similar dynamic within the GS North America coverage universe. Based on YTD changes to GS analysts' forecasts, we see aggregate earnings revisions (net income weighted) of 7.5% and 9.2% vs. median EPS revisions of 1.1% and 0.9%, for 2026 and 2027, respectively (we only consider names with positive expected earnings for this analysis). And on the performance side, on a market cap-weighted basis, our coverage is up 12% but the median stock is up 2.4% (only 54% of stocks are up YTD).

Even amidst this narrow breadth, a bottom-up analysis of our analysts' estimates suggests the old adage that “earnings drive stocks” continues to hold true over longer periods of time. In this recent earnings period (March period end), beats weren’t necessarily translating into stock performance in some sectors where questions persist (e.g. software, consumer discretionary). title_content.content: Directors' Cut is not managed as a portfolio, but what is the performance as if it was?

paragraph_content.content: Among the most frequent questions we get from investors is the portfolio performance of Directors' Cut. Despite our efforts to explain to investors why they should not view this list as a portfolio (we don't overlay risk metrics like liquidity, volatility, factors, or size based on those variables; we don't intentionally take sector views; we only update the list once a month), there is still curiosity on the efficacy of list performance in the aggregate and outside our standard metric of individual stock hit rate.

Below we illustrate the Conviction List Directors' Cut performance as if the list was in fact treated as an equal weighted portfolio since inception. In this illustrative portfolio, performance is calculated on a USD total return basis; rebalanced to equal weight on a monthly basis (alongside CL publication). If constituents change due to intra-month removals, the weights of stocks that are removed get redistributed among the remaining stocks in proportion of their existing weights. Performance is calculated using the first closing price after addition to the Conviction List or after removal from the Conviction List mimicking the incurrence of transaction costs.

Using these parameters, Directors' Cut has returned +28% over the last 12 months, outperforming the three benchmarks we track (relative to SPX -180bps, SPX EW +760 bps; GS rated coverage +30bps). title_content.content: Air Products & Chemicals Inc. (APD) - covered by Duffy Fischer

paragraph_content.content: A return-to-core company in a strong core end market

APD is one of the three global major industrial gas providers with new management focused on returning the company to its core competencies — an effort that Fischer expects to accelerate topline growth and yield stronger returns for investors. Industrial gas demand tends to track industrial production and industrial gas demand is near a trough. But if the US economy can avoid recession, a positive manufacturing inflection is likely, and APD should enter a prolonged beat-and-raise EPS cycle.

item_content.content: Core business can generate 10%+ through-the-cycle growth. The algorithm of through-the-cycle EPS growth for APD is anchored by 3% CAGR each from volume/market growth driven by industrial production; new project start-ups; and margin boosting price and efficiency gains versus input cost inflation; plus an additional 1% of EPS growth from debt reduction, stock buybacks or tuck-in M&A

Darrow decision should come by the end of FY26 (Sept). Investors have been waiting with increased uncertainty for the final decision on the Darrow blue H2/Ammonia project. Based on management comments, Fischer thinks the likelihood it goes forward is low but if it does it will be a solid return project. Regardless investors should know by September and certainty is likely to be a positive for the stock.

Higher oil price helps with underperforming coal gasification projects. APD has three coal gasification plants in China that have been poor return projects with almost no earnings contribution in 2025. The SoH issue has caused China's coal to chemicals businesses to see much better volume and spread opportunities, so those businesses should see significantly higher earnings in 2026. Separately, APD would like to dispose of two of those plants and the higher earnings profile should help that cause.

Cash flow positive. The company has indicated that its 3% organic growth target can be funded by $1.5bn in annual growth capex, significantly below its current run-rate of nearly $4bn — much of which is funding the blue/green portfolio which it is winding down. Once the large project build-out begins to wind down, look for the company to de-lever, paying down debt to get leverage near 2.0X Net Debt-to-EBITDA and investment grade (important for an industrial gas business).

paragraph_content.content: Fischer remains above consensus EPS for fiscal 2026 through 2028. He maintains his view of APD being able to narrow the multiple gap to LIN and potentially rerate as APD continues to deliver on previously stated strategic goals. This would be supported by delivering consistent earnings results over the next several quarters to prove out the reliability of the core business and provide reassurance around the helium business. title_content.content: Block Inc (XYZ) - covered by Will Nance

paragraph_content.content: A cash generating share gainer with an AI productivity enhancement story.

The holding company of Square and Cash App is one of the premier consumer neobank and payment platforms in the US and is on a path to higher profitability as it attracts more and stickier users to its platforms through wallet share expansion and product improvements in select verticals. Focus on: (1) accelerating customer acquisition trends for Square merchants, driven by new products and a more focused sales approach; (2) reduced lending growth in its Cash App business coupled with a focus on wallet share expansion with the app's heaviest users; and (3) margin improvement driven by top tier efficiency enabled by its recent 40% workforce reduction and embracing AI internally. Look for EPS growth of 64% in 2026 and 36% in 2027 to drive the stock higher from here.

item_content.content: Accelerating momentum in Square, led by field sales investments and product improvements to restaurant offering. Square has spent the last two years investing in its restaurant product offering (the restaurant-specific software suite that runs on Square devices), and building out its field sales organization. Look for accelerating growth in the number of merchants adopting Square to drive strong gross profit trends. Focus on: annualized New Volume Added (NVA) as the key forward looking indicator to measure the coming acceleration.
■ Moderating lending growth in Cash App and consistent spending led growth.

paragraph_content.content: Cash App has significantly expanded its short duration lending products, driving a gross profit acceleration from 10% to 38% in the most recent quarter. However, the remixing of growth towards lending has raised concern among some investors who are wary of a bad credit cycle. Look for concerns to fade as lending growth moderates in 2H26. Additionally, Cash App growth should increasingly remix towards higher multiple ‘Commerce Enablement’ revenue streams (i.e. swipe fees when Cash App customers spend on the Cash App debit card). Finally, Cash App is introducing a string of new products, including Cash App Green, a membership tier for highly active users. Look for continued strong growth in Cash App’s most active customer segment—what the company refers to as Primary Banking Active (PBA) users — resulting in strong consumer spending volumes and improved ARPUs.
■ Accelerating margin leverage from workforce reductions and AI-driven

efficiencies. XYZ recently announced a 40% headcount reduction to right-size its workforce and harness developer efficiency from the use of AI. These cost benefits are expected to ramp into 2H26 as headcount falls, and should drive accelerated margin benefits, helping to sustain elevated EPS growth in 2H26 and 2027. Nance views Block as an early adopter of AI tools and believes the company has effectively embedded AI into its workstreams, positioning it well to sustain product velocity while also improving workforce productivity.
Nance's 2027 EPS estimate is

ahead of consensus, driven by (1) stronger than expected Square spend volume growth; (2) sustained strong commerce enablement GP growth in Cash App, (see also “The way forward for Alt Managers: Reframing growth and valuation”); and (3) margin tailwinds from the company’s cost reduction measures.
12-month price target of \$95 is based on based on a 17x P/E target multiple on Q5-Q8 EPS estimates. Risks include: a worsening macro environment, increasing competition, and unfavorable regulation.

Key catalysts include: (1) New Volume Added traction as Square machines are rolled out in more restaurants; (2) evidence of decelerating lending growth and benign credit losses; (3) traction in its Cash App Green and Managed Accounts product launches; and (4) sustained higher margin follow-through from its 40% workforce reduction and AI efficiency implementations.

title_content.content: Brixmor Property Group (BRX) - covered by Caitlin Burrows

paragraph_content.content: Underappreciated growth and pricing power ahead

Brixmor Property Group (BRX) is an underappreciated strip center REIT whose upgraded real estate portfolio, growing occupancy & rental rates, and high-quality tenants are helping drive its best-in-class recurring ~5%+ annual FFO growth through 2028.

item_content.content: Realizing the SNO Pipeline. As of 1Q26, BRX maintains a significant signed-but-not-occupied (SNO) spread of 370bps ($67mn in annual base rents), where ~58% will commence in 2Q-4Q26, creating a tailwind to economic occupancy. Notably, a large portion of this pipeline is occupied by high quality tenants, including grocers and off-price retail concepts.

Record Pricing Power. Strong leasing activity is coming at a time when very little new supply is being built (unique vs. other property types). Burrows believes this combination of high demand and limited new supply should help drive rent growth: TTM total cash leasing spreads were +17.2%, including new lease spreads of +37.9%.

Accretive External Growth. BRX continues to pursue high-yielding redevelopment projects, with an in-process pipeline of $302.4mn and expected incremental NOI yield of 10%. Furthermore, the company remains active in capital recycling, completing $107.9mn in dispositions during 1Q26 (and $11.3mn subsequent to quarter-end) to enhance portfolio quality and growth, followed by two acquisitions in late May (link).

paragraph_content.content: While only slightly above consensus in 2026, that difference increases by 2028 as Burrows' higher occupancy assumptions and continued pricing power accumulate. Given BRX has a discounted multiple vs the REIT sector, she believes its above average ~5.0%+ annual earnings (FFO/share) growth rate through 2028 is not being appreciated by the market. However, as BRX executes on its strategy, the multiple could expand. With the significant SNO pipeline, effectively 100% fixed rate debt, consistently strong leasing spreads, and a stable tenant base, Burrows sees limited downside risk to estimates.

12-month price target of $35, based on a Q5-Q8 target AFFO multiple of 18.1x. Key downside risks include: Deterioration in the open air retail environment with more retailer bankruptcies (tariff-induced or not, including known struggling large national chains as well as local retailers); Lower demand for space, causing slower-than-expected improvements to occupancy and lower leasing spreads; Further increases in interest rates, increasing BRX's interest expense; Slower transaction markets leading to uncertainty around cap rates and valuation; and lower stabilization of reinvestment projects, lower average NOI yields, and/or higher maintenance capex and leasing costs.

Continued realization (and backfill) of the \$67mn SNO pipeline into billed occupancy, potential upward revisions to 2026 FFO/SS NOI guidance with earnings, and incremental disclosures made during Nareit (Burrows and her team will meet with BRX on 6/2/2026).

item_content.content: ■ Strong visibility into AI revenue growth. Broadcom continues to see accelerating demand for its AI semiconductor solutions across both networking and XPUs. Better than feared margins. In addition, we believe the company's constructive commentary regarding component supply should help Broadcom maintain its current margin structure on its AI products in the medium term.

paragraph_content.content: Schneider continues to believe the Street is underestimating the amount of momentum in Broadcom's AI optical networking business. His FY27 non-GAAP EPS (ex SBC) estimate of $21.00 is 14% above the Street.

title_content.content: Carlisle Companies Inc. (CSL) - covered by Sue Maklari

paragraph_content.content: Value stock on the cusp of an earnings growth inflection.

Demand for the roofing, insulation, and waterproofing building products that CSL makes is fairly muted but Sue Maklari sees a path to a positive top-line inflection in 2026, even if non-residential construction activity remains fairly dormant. Maklari forecasts a 1% yoy increase in sales in 2Q26, followed by a continued recovery throughout 2H resulting in a 2% increase for 2026. Alongside tech-driven cost efficiencies, and a boost from buybacks, Maklari looks for EPS growth of 8% this year accelerating to 14% in 2027. With the stock trading at a NTM P/E of 16x vs an average of 18x since completing the strategic shift to a pure-play building products company in 2024, she expects upside as investors gain greater confidence around the path for earnings.

item_content.content: - Inventories bottoming as new products are arriving. Channel inventories are below historical norms coming into the spring and CSL is poised to lap a $50mn destock later this year. The company is also introducing a series of new products, including ThermaThin 7 polyiso insulation, which combined should drive volume growth and improve margins. In all, increasing R&D spend is contributing to the expected launch of 10+ new offerings in 2026 with a focus on technological advancements allowing for greater content per square foot over time, and contributing to Carlisle-specific price elasticity.

Cost focus and efficiency to boost margins. Look for cost improvements to offset operating headwinds from flat volumes. Management is focused on implementing greater automation and integrating technology solutions to reduce scrap and changeover time in its manufacturing facilities without sacrificing quality and safety. Maklari conservatively expects the consolidated EBITDA margin to bottom in 2Q (down 112bp YOY) before gradually improving to finish 2026 up 22bp at 24.6%.

Clean balance sheet provides growth optionality and shareholder returns. CSL's business model should generate a FCF margin in excess of 15%, and Maklari forecasts $783m of FCF in 2026. Including the guide for $1bn of share repurchases this year, Maklari estimates CSL will return $1.2bn to shareholders in the form of buybacks and dividends in 2026 – equivalent to ~9% of its market cap – with potential upside (given the current net debt-to-EBITDA of 1.7X). As sellers adjust their expectations to more closely align to current conditions, she looks for an eventual resumption of M&A activity, providing potential upside to her estimates over time.

Upside to CWT margins despite the ongoing housing pressures. This is led by self-help initiatives as Carlisle leverages its well-established playbook to realize greater productivity and efficiency without sacrificing quality. Maklari believes her 2026 estimate for the segment adj. EBITDA margin at 18.4%, up 113bps YoY, could prove conservative. Moreover, she sees a path to notable expansion once volumes recover and higher incremental margins are fully realized.
■ Confidence in ability to offset inflation. In response to the move in energy prices

paragraph_content.content: over the last few months, Carlisle announced two 5-8% price increases on non-res roofing materials effective in April and July and increased the freight surcharge $150 to $750 effective May 11. This comes as petrochemical feedstocks and transportation costs continue to move higher. We note peers have taken similar actions giving us confidence in realizations in the back half of 2026 and supporting upside risks to our estimates.

Well-positioned to mitigate competitive environment. The company's value-based strategy remains a priority, leveraging innovation, service and training excellence, to be a preferred supplier. Maklari believes these differentiators will protect Carlisle's market share as new entrants seek to compete on price.

12-month price target of $450 is based on 15.3x Maklari's Q5-Q8 adj. EBITDA forecast. Risks include: (1) an increase in raw material costs and the inability to pass them through, (2) failure to execute on key strategic initiatives, including the closure and successful integration of acquisitions, (3) efforts to drive greater productivity and efficiencies do not meet expectations, (4) loss or change in order patterns from key customers, and (5) increased competition should newer entrants seek to gain greater share.

title_content.content: Casella Waste Systems Inc. (CWST) - covered by Adam Bubes
Sustainable growth, with margin expansion ahead

paragraph_content.content: Adam Bubes sees scope for a sustained, mid-single-digit percentage organic EBITDA CAGR at CWST, driven by its Solid Waste pricing algo, with additional upside from SG&A savings and M&A synergies. CWST also offers the most M&A growth runway in Bubes' Waste coverage. Valuation has moved from a premium to in line with peers to a discount over the last year following integration challenges with the acquisition of GFL's Mid-Atlantic assets. But, with the integration now largely complete, and with customers transitioned to CWST's new lead-to-cash system, the focus is shifting to synergy realization.

- Margin expansion opportunity. CWST has a track record of pricing ahead of inflation, with pricing averaging a ~150 bps spread to CPI (less food and energy) annually over the last five years. Look for the favorable pricing backdrop to continue, underpinned by contract flexibility (70–75% of CWST's book can be repriced at will) and industry consolidation (the top four public players control >60% of landfill market share and >50% of collection market share). Beyond pricing, CWST recently outlined the potential for above-trend base business margin expansion over the next 2-3 years, supported by ~$30mn of identified cost opportunities, including $15mn of Mid-Atlantic integration synergies and $15mn of G&A cost reduction.

- Scope for value added M&A. CWST augments earnings power by driving local consolidation at value-enhancing multiples and capturing meaningful pricing and operational synergies on acquired assets. When collection bolt-ons are completed in existing markets, CWST benefits from increased local market share once assets are integrated into the footprint. Margin expansion is driven by improved route density, SG&A reduction, internalization of collection volumes at landfills, and automation. Over the last five years, M&A has contributed ~12% to revenue growth on average, and Bubes sees continued runway ahead, with >40% of the collection industry still privately owned.

- Reduced commodity and volume risk relative to peers. 100% of CWST's revenue is derived from Recycling and Solid Waste, compared to peers that have some exposure to more volatile ancillary business lines such as Medical Waste or E&P Waste. CWST also has the lowest recycling price and landfill gas price risk of his Waste coverage. CWST benefits from a differentiated commodity surcharge to collection customers, which floats inversely to recycling prices. As a result, CWST has the lowest recycling commodity exposure across his coverage (10% move in commodities translating to <0.2% impact on EBITDA). On landfill gas, CWST has four projects currently online in the early stages of ramping, representing potential upside to estimates. Importantly, CWST has invested no capital in these projects, instead giving 100% equity to its development partner and recouping only a royalty payment.

title_content.content: Celestica Inc. (CLS) - covered by Michael Ng
Scaled tech hardware provider with a design kicker

paragraph_content.content: CLS's strong engineering capabilities, combined with its ability to quickly and reliably scale production, provides it with a competitive advantage over other ODM and EMS providers in supplying equipment to data centers. Mike Ng expects CLS to benefit from ongoing capex growth amongst hyperscale and other large AI players, where the company has demonstrated its ability to win customer programs in cutting edge technology (e.g., 800G and 1.6T networking switches), and should continue to gain traction over time in custom ASIC (TPU) server programs.

Tier 1 data center supplier. ~80% of CLS's revenue comes from data center equipment (servers, switching, and storage) where demand should benefit from ongoing data center buildouts, which should drive cloud provider data center equipment spend to grow at a 31% 5-year 2025-2030 CAGR, per 650 Group. CLS is the market share leader in 800G data center switching (28% revenue share as of 4Q25 per 650 Group), which should advantage the company amidst ongoing hyperscale upgrades to 800G & 1.6T data center switching speeds in 2026-2027. Additionally, CLS's integration of design and manufacturing across networking and compute puts it in an enviable position to address growing interest towards more rack-level solutions — as illustrated by CLS' Digital Native full-rack solution contract win.

- Higher margins custom design. CLS should be able to increase its data center (CCS) segment operating margins over time through its growing ability to deliver value-add design work to its solutions. While ODM work comprised ~7% of the company's revenue in 2017, Celestica's ongoing investments in design & engineering capabilities have allowed the company to grow its ODM revenue share to ~41% in 2025, driving CCS segment operating margins from ~3% to ~8% over the same period. Notably, CLS' recent Digital Native full-rack solution contract win marks the company's first ODM server win.

Cyclical upside from industrials. Growing demand for clean energy generation and storage, industrial automation, defense equipment, as well as sustained demand for aerospace equipment, healthcare and life science research tools, should all benefit CLS' wide-ranging footprint across its ATS segment in the years ahead — especially as many of these end markets inflect positively, coming off of cyclical bottoms. These exposures also have strong competitive moats and provide reliable ballast, supporting CLS's faster growing data center end markets.

■ Superior growth profile. Celestica expects 70% revenue growth in its CCS segment (which sells networking switches, servers, and storage) in 2026 based on demand visibility through its deep relationships with hyperscale customers with multi-year investment planning cycles. As such, Ng expects Celestica should grow overall revenue from $12.4bn in 2025 to $55.4bn in 2030 at a 35% 5-year CAGR, with EPS growth outpacing at a 40% 2025-2030 CAGR.

Ng forecasts ~$16.12/$20.24 of EPS for 2027/28 (vs. Visible Alpha Consensus Data at $15.03/$19.41), with further room for upward EPS revisions driven by CLS's exposure to key growth verticals including: (1) Google TPU-related demand (CLS is an EMS assembly partner for Google); (2) additional custom-ASIC program wins (CLS is the single-sourced manufacturing and design partner for a full-rack solution for a large digital native customer with a custom ASIC, expected to ramp in 1H27).

12-month target price of $475 is based on a NTM+1Y target P/E multiple of 28X. Downside risks include: continued competition from branded data center equipment OEMs and ODMs, which could pressure market share; AI server market competitive intensity, which can pressure AI server margins; high customer concentration could cause revenue volatility; potential declines in data center investment demand; reductions in CLS's ability to win higher margin design-deals, which could limit CLS' ability to grow EBIAT margins over time; worsening supply chain constraints on switching silicon and memory could pressure revenue upside; and volatility in end-market demand within CLS' ATS segment.

Key catalysts for the stock include: (a) continued upwards revisions of hyperscale capex, (b) potential 2028 outlook introduction in Fall 2026, (c) announcements of broader adoption of CLS' customers' custom AI chip architectures (e.g. Google TPU by external players), (d) production ramp of custom designed rack for CLS' digital native customer in 1H27, or (e) new custom design wins across networking and server equipment for AI players.

Bank efficiency program ('reimagine the bank') to drive $450m of pre-tax run-rate benefit by 2028. CFG's program is focused on optimizing client service to be less costly and improving its branch network. Nash is looking for higher loan growth with loans growing ~5% YoY to ~$149.3bn vs. consensus of ~$148.4bn given higher core commercial loan growth, improving private bank loans in consumer and commercial, as well as a slowing of run-off activity which could drive upside to EPS. Lastly, Nash expects CFG to repurchase $2.0bn of additional shares through 2027 while maintaining a ~10.5% CET1 ratio, but given CFG's expectation to manage capital towards a 10%–10.5% CET1 ratio over time, there could be upside if CFG looks to further lever its capital base.

Look for the company to highlight the expected benefits from the proposed Basel rules which should be a larger benefit relative to peers given its loan composition and could point to upside for share repurchase expectations through 2027. title_content.content: Big oil shifting to harvest mode

paragraph_content.content: Mehta sees COP experiencing a positive free cash flow inflection through the end of the decade as it transitions from a long period of heavy project investment to boost its oil reserves into a new period of ‘investment harvesting’ characterized by major projects coming online and capex diminishing — all coming alongside what he sees as improving oil supply/demand fundamentals. Look for COP to realize accelerating free cash flow growth at a higher rate of change than large-cap peers, and potential further upside if global oil fundamentals improve even more. Strong free cash flow generation should also support consistent shareholder returns while sustaining a strong balance sheet. Please see here for takeaways from our recent Boston trip with CEO, Mr. Ryan Lance.

- Project pipeline coming online. COP's Willow oil project in Alaska is now ~50% complete, with four wells fully permitted, and on track for first oil in early 2029. At the same time, the company's LNG projects (NFE/NFS in Qatar and Port Arthur in Texas) continue to progress. Despite recent disruptions in the Middle East, worker retention and pre-purchased equipment have broadly kept the NFE project in Qatar on-track. Mehta continues to favor the company's lower geopolitical risk profile relative to global peers given portfolio concentration in OECD areas such as Alaska, the Lower 48, and Canada. Separately, management is enhancing efficiency in the Lower 48, drilling additional 3-mile plus lateral length wells and adding a rig in the Permian to keep pace with completions.

New projects + costs savings = $7bn. The company’s four major growth projects (NFE, NFS, Port Arthur, Willow), combined with ~$1bn in cost reductions and margin enhancements, should drive ~$7bn in incremental free cash flow by 2029 at $70/b WTI. Mehta expects free cash flow to continue to grow into 2030, estimating an ~11% free cash flow yield at $75/b Brent. He sees further upside to estimates if major projects, particularly Willow, coincide with a longer-dated oil upcycle as non-OPEC supply growth slows and solid demand growth continues.

Balance sheet strength facilitates capital returns. COP management is committed to a healthy combination of sustaining a strong balance sheet alongside returning cash to shareholders in the form of dividends and buybacks. As cash flow inflects positively, look for COP to return ~45% of cash from operations (in-line with its long-term track record), while growing the base dividend as free cash flow break-even falls into the low US$30s/WTI bbl by the end of the decade. Mehta forecasts over a ~30% increase in total annual capital returns to shareholders by 2030.

Mehta estimates a ~24% free cash flow per share CAGR from 2025-2030 at a long-term Brent price of $75/b. If he holds commodity prices from 2025 flat, Mehta estimates a free cash flow per share CAGR from 2025-2030 closer to ~20%, highlighting the company's ability to compound value in a commodity-neutral environment.

12-month price target of $144 results from a P/E, EV/DACF, and DCF-based valuation methodology. Mehta applies a target 14.5x P/E multiple and 8.5x EV/DACF multiple on mid-cycle estimates. To capture the uplift in free cash flow, he incorporates a 20-year DCF with an 8% cost of capital. Key risks include commodity prices, capital spend, and operational execution.

Key milestones ahead include the sealift of processing modules from the Gulf Coast to Alaska for the Willow project, and the start-up of NFE. Additional areas of investor focus include: (a) Lower 48 activity, (b) commodity price realizations, (c) capital spend efficiency, and (d) LNG strategy.

title_content.content: Dick's Sporting Goods (DKS) - covered by Kate McShane

paragraph_content.content: At the corner of retail/eCommerce's blurring lines, restructuring, and the health and fitness craze

With its acquisition of Foot Locker (FL) in September, DKS is positioned to be the retailer on the front lines of resuscitating the sneaker category, with a shared goal with key vendor NKE of bringing back the excitement of in-store new product releases, reducing low-cost inventory across old FL stores, re-energizing vendor relationships, and providing a platform for higher end, higher margin sneaker sales. Additionally, DKS remains at the forefront of a broader health, fitness, and athleisure trend that is showing no signs of abating in the year ahead. Overtime, look for DKS to bring up gross margins at FL by ~300bp or more as it narrows the gap with DKS' superior margin profile.

item_content.content: Sneakers first. The acquisition of FL last summer comes with risks as DKS still has to show the market they can grow sales at the Foot Locker banners. But an improved store experience along with an assortment carrying more relevant styles, higher brand heat and an improved shopping experience should make Foot Locker meaningfully more competitive. New FL Fast Break stores are already reflecting a less cluttered environment and some higher heat merchandise, with a more comprehensive change in product offering expected by Back to School 2026. In 1Q, Foot Locker delivered its first positive comp (+0.6%) since 4Q24, with the US Foot Locker banner at +6.4%, along with solid early results from the Fast Break initiative (+DD comps in 1Q).

Core DKS remains solid. Following 1Q top line outperformance with a Dick's comp of +6.0%, management increased Dick's comp guidance at the midpoint to 2.5-4.0% in FY26, reflecting the ongoing consumer attraction to everything health and fitness. Additionally, McShane believes that concerns around restructuring efforts at FL cannibalizing sales at Dick's branded stores are overdone. Overlapping brands at the two stores averages only 35% and discounting so far has not been overly aggressive at FL.

- More blurring lines. DKS' investments in Game Changer and Dick's Media Network, continue to grow faster and at higher margins than the base business. These efforts to leverage DKS customer base into asset light revenue streams and advertising dollars should continue to bear fruit as the blurring lines between eCommerce, retailing, and advertising only get blurrier.

paragraph_content.content: McShane's on-the-ground research of new FL test stores as well as the leveraging of big data to assess the market opportunity and pricing dynamics of the sneaker industry provide unique insights into a retailer in transition.

12-month price target of $277, based on a downside/base/upside case relative target P/E multiples of 60%/65%/70%. Downside risks include: a weaker demand environment amidst economic uncertainty; delays in improving the Foot Locker business; potential for inventory overhang and discounting in the industry; DTC initiatives from major brands; weaker sports participation trends.

McShane expects some upside risk to Q2 Dick's results from the World Cup. She also looks for an acceleration at Foot Locker on the top and bottom line around back-to-school in 2026 when the impact of DKS's merchandising changes are visible in Foot Locker stores, in part due to higher brand heat products leading to full price sell-through and a lower level of markdowns for the banner.

title_content.content: DoorDash Inc. (DASH) - covered by Eric Sheridan

paragraph_content.content: Online delivery leader with leverage to a healthy consumer looking for everything to be delivered

DASH is well positioned both cyclically and secularly as we step into 2026, where our economists forecast above-consensus US GDP growth. On the cyclical side, Sheridan sees DASH's revenue growth being sustained by a healthy consumer – especially for the middle income and above cohorts – looking for more things to be delivered to their door. At the secular level, DASH is at the nexus of blurring lines between advertising and eCommerce as well as the localization of eCommerce. Look for the company to accelerate topline growth to 30% in 2026E even as net cash grows by 50% – putting the stock in the “sweet spot” of capital-light revenue expansion.

Cyclical tailwinds. Our economists look for a stable US consumer in 2026, boosted by real income growth supported by above-consensus GDP growth. The outlook is particularly encouraging for middle-income and above income cohorts. As the consumer remains strong, Sheridan sees the potential for upside top-line growth – also helped by secular exposures.

Secular tailwinds. The widening out of use cases from food delivery to grocery delivery to local commerce initiatives is presenting one of the most compelling secular growth themes for delivery companies such as DASH. And DASH is also at the nexus of blurring lines between advertising and eCommerce. In 2026, look for DASH to execute on an increasingly wide array of retailer/inventory partners that continue to broaden out the scope for compounded growth (and the pace and cadence of that slope to drive sustained duration of that growth).

Financials to go with the themes. In a world that is requiring more and more capital to generate tougher and tougher revenue growth, DASH's business model is built as a pure eCommerce internet engine. Sheridan forecasts revenue growth accelerating to 30% in 2026E from 28.5% in 2025. And this acceleration will only fuel a cleaner balance sheet as the resulting $4bn-plus in free cash flow only needs to feed ~$700m of capex, leaving over $3bn of cash to distribute to shareholders and build a larger cash cushion.

Sheridan's bottom-up framework on the incremental order volume and GOV contribution between international, US core restaurant and new verticals helps frame his view that local commerce will remain a key growth driver in the broader business. In addition, he believes DASH's 2026 investment cycle as a compelling driver toward international growth & scaling the company's local commerce business. The local commerce business is expected to drive engagement, increased frequency (order volume) and retention on the platform in the coming years.

12-month target price of \$280 is based on an equal blend of (1) a 36x target EV/GAAP EBITDA multiple applied to GSe NTM + 1-year estimates and (2) a modified DCF using a target 28X EV/FCF-SBC multiple applied to GSe NTM + 4-years estimates discounted back 3 years. Key risks include: (1) the consumer and potential for slower growth for food delivery; (2) higher levels of marketing spend required to drive both demand and supply growth in its marketplace; (3) regulation; (4) competition; (5) international expansion; (6) earnings volatility; and (7) volatility caused by the global macroeconomic environment and investor risk appetite for growth stocks.

2Q26 earnings; Key areas of investor focus include (a) health of the consumer / end demand trends, (b) updates to the duration of incremental tech investments, and (c) momentum in local commerce growth (Grocery and Retail).

title_content.content: Duke Energy Corp. (DUK) – covered by Carly Davenport

paragraph_content.content: Well-positioned with regulators, suppliers, and its own management team.

DUK is making regulatory progress that should support strong growth in the Carolinas and Florida. Additionally, as the utility ramps up its development of greater electricity generation capacity, capex should be supported by its partnership with nat gas turbine supplier GEV which should provide it with better access to gas turbines — critical to actually building the new power capacity. Finally, Davenport believes newer leadership is paving the way for a unified strategic path to more sustainable growth.

- GEV partnership provides capex advantage. Building out new electrical generation capacity has become expensive and time-consuming given supply chain constraints. But DUK's ability to build at scale through its partnership with GEV gives it a competitive advantage to bring on gas generation quicker and more cost effectively than its peers. Through DUK and GEV's partnership, the utility secured 20 natural gas turbines to meet growing demand needs into the 2030s and expects delivery on the turbines for its NC Person County CC units in 2H2026. Duke expects to spend $103 bn in capex over the next five years, with about
going towards the grid and about
going towards new generation.

Regulatory clarity emerges. Key constraints for DUK have been its challenged balance sheet due to regulatory lag and the storms that occur in the company's service territory. But the improved regulatory environment in the company's service territories have paved the way for DUK to become a more premium utility due to its supportive earnings growth and the ability to recover costs in a timely manner. In particular, favorable settlements/outcomes in the Carolinas and Florida in recent rate cases put DUK on a better path to higher and more predictable returns.

Discounted valuation. DUK currently trades at a 7% discount to premium peers, below its historical discount average. But DUK is positioned to grow earnings even faster than it has in the past – 8% CAGR versus 5-year historical growth rate of 3% – suggesting that it should see multiple expansion to the premium peer average. FactSet consensus EPS estimates are also 2%/4% below GS 2027/2028 estimates.
Davenport's estimates are

above consensus, on average, for 2026-2029. She is more optimistic on DUK's improving balance sheet outlook, which should be supportive of above-trend earnings growth going forward relative to history. Davenport believes the progress the company has made on regulatory mechanisms and ROEs, as well as its load growth underpinned by increasing capex opportunities in its service territories, as reflected by its updated investment plans, including the ability to build more gas power in the near term, should solidify DUK as a premium utility from a valuation perspective.

12-month target price of $145 is based on a P/E multiple of 19.5x on Davenport's Q5-Q8 estimates to capture the upside opportunities around generation capex and improved regulatory position. Key downside risks include: DUK's balance sheet not improving; regulatory uncertainty from its outstanding rate cases; and any decline in the strong load growth forecast impacting expected earnings growth.

DUK reaching its 15% FFO/debt target; the second closing of the Florida asset sale by December 2026; rate case resolution in North Carolina; progress on the Carolinas Resource Plan with an order expected by the end of 2026 and a final order on its South Carolina IRP update; execution on EPS results and power generation asset additions on time could all be positive catalysts for shares.

title_content.content: Golar LNG (GLNG) - covered by John Mackay

paragraph_content.content: Underappreciated, catalyst-rich growth story with dependable economics

GLNG operates floating LNG (FLNG) production units that have the ability to move around the world to capture nat gas from offshore extraction projects. GLNG has one unit operating, a second that is completing one contract and is being remobilized to start its next, and is constructing a third one (all fully contracted). John Mackay thinks this capacity expansion should drive contracted EBITDA roughly 3x higher by YE28; and a FCF yield of
growing to the mid-teens in outer years. Adding a fourth unit (final investment decision to be reached later this year) would only further sustain the company's growth.

item_content.content: Advantageous market position secures funding and provides a competitive moat. GLNG's status as the only public pure-play owner and operator of FLNG production units supports the company's ability to effectively fully contract its LNG liquefaction capacity under long-term, take-or-pay contracts, which are structured to provide downside protection in a softer global gas price environment.

Visible ramp to a tripling of EBITDA. GLNG’s fully funded project backlog is set to drive contracted EBITDA approximately 3x higher by the end of 2028 to an annual run-rate of $800m versus 2025 of ~$260mn. The backlog is fully contracted under take-or-pay contracts including ~$150mn from FLNG Gimi contracted in West Africa for BP/KOS, $285mn for FLNG Hilli in Argentina, and $400mn for FLNG Fuji in Argentina. These long-term, 20-year contracts, include upside optionality on global gas prices without domestic US gas price risks, which combined with the fully funded nature of the projects, creates a de-risked lens into a long-term growth outlook that is still underappreciated by the market.

- Fourth vessel option upside. In addition to the two fully operating vessels and a third under construction (and fully contracted), GLNG is approaching a FID decision on building a fourth vessel, which Mackay thinks could come in 3Q26. Depending on the vessel size and charter rates, Mackay estimates that a mid-sized (Mark II) vessel with the same contract terms as FLNG Fuji could represent ~50% upside to the current EBITDA backlog, or ~$12/sh fundamental upside to the stock. Amid recent global LNG supply disruptions, Mackay is incremental constructive on a fourth vessel moving forward this summer and potentially a fifth vessel moving forward in 1H27.

paragraph_content.content: Mackay's differentiated view includes: 1) a clear path to follow on steps towards a fourth vessel FID, and 2) the potential for GLNG to monetize early some of its commodity-linked upside options embedded in its current contracts. On the former, he believes that while GLNG is not likely to place a complete new vessel order before locking in commercial contracts, Mackay believes the company is tracking well to achieve FID by 3Q26, particularly since the company placed orders for long-lead items in May 2026. Furthermore, amid the tighter supply/demand balances following global LNG supply disruptions, Mackay is increasingly constructive on the potential for a fifth vessel to come ~6 months after the fourth, or sometime 1H27. On the second item, he sees potential incremental upside from Golar exploring the ability to crystallize value on the commodity upside option baked into their contracts (+$70mn/yr of cash flow every $1/mmbtu >$8/mmbtu gas pricing on two of their contracts) – a piece of the story that the public market tends to not assign value to, which could potentially allow GLNG to start to pre-fund capex for the fourth vessel.

12-month price target of $66 is based on a fundamental valuation at an 85% weight based on an unlevered DCF discounted at a 9.5% WACC with a 10.5x terminal year EBITDA multiple, and an M&A theoretical value at a 15% weight based on an unlevered DCF (with a 75% inclusion of a fifth FLNG Mark II vessel) discounted at a 9.0% WACC with a 10.5x exit year terminal value EBITDA multiple. Downside risks include: (1) modest exposure to lower global gas pricing, (2) counterparty concentration and geopolitical risk, (3) higher than expected conversion costs and/or longer than expected conversion timelines, (4) early contract termination, (5) complex and/or atypical financing arrangements weighing on perceived transparency for investors, and (6) lower than guaranteed operational capacity.

item_content.content: ■ Strategic alternative launched. On 3/25/26, GLNG formally announced it has launched a strategic review of the company with a focus on accelerating the growth pipeline of FLNG vessels (Mackay thinks this could include a fourth and potentially fifth vessel, which would be upside to his outlook) and maximizing shareholder value, with potential alternatives including a sale of the company as well as other potential outcomes.

- Fourth Vessel FID. The FID for a fourth FLNG vessel is possible by 3Q26. Management ordered long-lead items for the pre-FID fourth vessel in May 2026, which we see as progress towards full commercialization.

Crystallization of commodity option value. Golar is exploring the ability to crystallize value on the commodity upside option baked into their contracts (+$70mn/yr of cash flow every $1/mmbtu >$8/mmbtu gas pricing on two of their contracts) which could drive funding clarity for a fourth FID. This could include locking in commodity upside from hedging volumes committed to long-term offtake agreements signed by SESA (2 mtpa have been signed to-date, SESA is targeting signing an additional 3 mtpa of capacity).

■ Project ramp-up and de-risking. Successful construction execution on the first vessel, FLNG Hilli, next year for its refurbishment and the second vessel, FLNG Fuji, will de-risk the current project pipeline, supporting line of sight to achieve 3x growth in annual run-rate EBITDA by YE28.

- Shareholder returns. While line of sight to executing the project backlog supports capital allocation flexibility later this decade, in the near-term, management can lean into opportunistic buybacks following the recent $150mn share repurchase authorization announced alongside 3Q25 results.

paragraph_content.content: Steady, structural growth opportunity in traditional retail brokerage

James Yaro believes IBKR is successfully innovating the crowded, and competitive, retail broker landscape. The retail broker landscape has been somewhat volatile, but IBKR's exposure to more traditional verticals (vs. crypto) offers steady, structural growth, with potential upside from expansion into nascent verticals, including prime brokerage and prediction markets. Further, industry retail equity trading trends appear to have inflected positively in May for the first time since early March, rising 8% MoM TD.

Organic Account Growth. Yaro expects IBKR to continue to deliver robust organic account growth as the company continues to scale its global presence (~85% of new accounts are ex-US with broad diversification across countries, with the largest non-US account growth country at only 5% of app downloads) amid a strong retail trading backdrop – with only 4.9mn accounts as of April 2026, he believes IBKR has low single digit account market share in each of the key global regions in which it operates, the Americas, Europe, and Asia. IBKR continues to invest heavily in its product set and efficiency, with an enhanced focus on increasing marketing spend to support account growth. Yaro forecasts a 25% 2025-28E average account CAGR (which compares to only 7% for peers), and a 13% top-line CAGR, with de minimis AI and crypto price risk, unlike many peer brokers.

TAM expansion opportunity. In addition to its core retail business, Yaro sees a number of nascent growth opportunities for IBKR, including prime brokerage, prediction markets, as well as a healthy introducing broker (white labeling its brokerage tech to banks and wealth managers) pipeline. Look for IBKR to lean into ForecastEx, a Designated Contract Market (DCM - an exchange), as a core organic growth vector, planning to broaden its contract set.

Profitability. The company continues to incorporate AI across the organization, seeking to improve client experience, and drive back-office automation and company efficiency. IBKR also offers a unique 75%+ pre-tax margin profile driving robust capital generation, and Yaro thinks margins are sustainable from 2025E-28E, despite continued investment and marketing. He also sees upside optionality from potential inorganic growth, as the company has begun to focus on deploying some of its rapidly growing excess capital, which is >$8bn currently (or 6% of current market cap).

Yaro projects stronger platform expansion for IBKR than the Street, with 2% higher 2026E/27E average earning assets, and 1% stronger 2026E net new accounts, resulting in 2026E/27E revenue 1%/2% ahead of consensus estimates.

12m target of $102 is based on 35X Yaro's Q5-Q8 P/E target multiple. Downside risks include account growth deceleration; fewer trades/account; lower revenue/trade; faster interest rate cuts than expected; market volatility and margin loans; margin compression
required to sustain account growth.

Yaro anticipates investor attention around IBKR's monthly metric releases, where he expects the company to continue demonstrating healthy account growth and balance sheet expansion, which should drive both transaction and net interest revenues.

title_content.content: Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) – covered by Asad Haider

paragraph_content.content: Navigating a patent cliff to a higher stock price.

JNJ is a stable, defensive grower with the industry's strongest balance sheet allowing for continued high-ROIC investments in the Innovative Medicines segment to augment revenue growth. JNJ's successful navigation of a major patent cliff (Stelara) on the back of multiple new product cycles has made it one of the top performing pharmaceutical companies (+43% in 2025, 11% YTD 2026), and Haider believes there is further upside. In our February NDR, JNJ's CEO struck a decidedly confident tone in the outlook for the company, potential double-digit growth exiting the decade supported by multiple product cycles across oncology, immunology, neuroscience, potential milvexian success in SSP and AF, as well as conviction in accelerating growth in its MedTech franchise. Finally, JNJ's sector-high balance sheet capacity of +$80bn positions it well to further supplement growth through acquisitions, where management continues to express earlier stage deals as the sweet spot.

Stelara LOE has been manageable. JNJ's immunology drug, Stelera, went off patent in 2025 opening the market to lower cost generics and jeopardizing $10bn+ of revenue for the company. But JNJ has a next-generation drug, Tremfya, that the company has been focused on to replace Stelera that has significantly offset the loss of revenue from Stelera. Post a strong 2025, recent Tremfya prescription trends point to continued strength YTD in 2026, with continued share-taking in IBD against Skyrizi per the advantage of subcutaneous induction. Beyond Tremfya, the company has also already been making progress on its combination strategy in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), where JNJ-4804 (combination of Tremfya and Simponi) has recently released encouraging Ph2 data in the refractory patient population and could be positioned as a revenue cycle management strategy for Tremfya.

JNJ has multiple product cycles. JNJ is in the inning of multiple new biopharma product cycles across a wide range of therapeutics areas, across multiple myeloma (Tecvayli + Darzalex combination, Talvey), immunology (Tremfya, Icotyde), lung cancer (Rybrevant + Lazcluze), bladder cancer (Inlexzo), and neuroscience (Caplyta), where Haider estimates meaningful overall revenue opportunities with upside potential. Specifically, the trajectory of the Icotyde launch in psoriasis will be key to the stock, where the company has recently framed it as potentially one of the company's largest products (suggests >$10bn). Here, our KOL diligence continues to suggest broad-based excitement about the drugs profile, and the potential to expand into psoriatic arthritis and IBD.

Inorganic growth opportunities. In addition to in-house drug revenue visibility, JNJ is also positioned to supplement organic growth through strategic M&A, utilizing its sector-leading balance sheet capacity of +$80bn. The recent acquisition of Intra-Cellular Therapies highlights JNJ's aim of being the #1 neuroscience company by 2030. At our most recent NDR, management continues to see meaningful BD opportunities across earlier stage deals.

Haider believes consensus is under-appreciating the trajectory of the Innovative Medicine business (~64% of revenues vs. MedTech 36%, but a disproportionate 77% of profit, and hence more important for the materiality of the stock) as the company laps the Stelara cliff into numerous new product cycles across multiple large markets such as IBD, psoriasis, neuropsych, multiple myeloma, bladder cancer and EGFR mutated non-small-cell lung cancer. The biggest push back remains on valuation: JNJ's FY2 multiples has inflected from ~13.5x since Haider's April 2025 initiation to ~18x, consistent with a main message from his initiation that historical analogs show that Pharma stock multiples tend to trough ~1-year ahead of major LOE. However, Haider believes that ultimately multiples follows the trajectory of revenue growth, where his estimates remain above consensus and we believe that the continued commercial momentum could provide investors increasing confidence/clarity towards the company's goal of double-digit top-line growth in the later part of the decade (vs. Consensus 7-8%).

12-month price target of $275 is derived by applying a 20.0x PE multiple on Q5-Q8/EPS. Key risks include: The ramp of new products could be slower than expected, resulting in less revenue to replenish declining products. Further uncertainty related to the Talc litigation could result in higher-than-expected payouts and hamper multiples. A more difficult-to-navigate external environment related to macro and tariffs could create downside to Haider's estimates.

Key catalysts include: Icotyde launch in psoriasis, where there is wide excitement among the physician community following the approval; Caplyta Launch in aMDD following recent approval, where management believes that aMDD could be the largest of the indications across schinzophrenia and biopolar I and biopolar II; milvexian Librexia AF and Librexia STROKE readouts in 2026 where expectations continue to be mixed following recent discontinuation in ACS but positive readthrough from Bayer's asundexian; and nipocalimab Ph3 data in Warm Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia and Ph2 data in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus where we believe the franchise remains underappreciated.
